This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For what values of $0\leq m<n$ is there a complete sequence $A=\{a_1\leq a_2\leq \cdots\}$ of integers such that
 $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but 
 $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements? 
#348: [ErGr80]
number theory | 
complete sequences
The Fibonacci sequence $1,1,2,3,5,\ldots$ shows that $m=1$ and $n=2$ is possible. The sequence of powers of $2$ shows that $m=0$ and $n=1$ is possible. The case $m=2$ and $n=3$ is not known.
van Doorn has shown that no such sequence exists for $2\leq m<n$ if we interpret complete in the strong sense that\[\left\{ \sum_{n\in B}n : \textrm{ for all finite }B\subset A\right\}=\mathbb{N}.\]Erdős and Graham most likely meant the weaker notion of completeness which allows finitely many exceptions, however.
Additional thanks to: Wouter van Doorn

 Some computational findings on the (2,3) case that may be useful to others (code and certificates available on request). There is a natural intermediate object between "no such sequence" and a full witness: a multiset that remains complete after removing any two elements, while infinitely many specific triples destroy completeness permanently. Take the Fibonacci values 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … with multiplicities 3, 2, then alternating 2, 1 — i.e. 1,1,1,2,2,3,3,5,8,8,13,21,21,34,55,55,89,… Removing any two elements leaves it complete (exhaustively verified at low levels, extended upward by a periodicity argument; in our checks the surviving multisets in fact have no exceptions at all), while removing a doubled value together with its successor breaks it forever: e.g. after deleting {8,8,13}, the remaining elements below 21 sum to 18, so 19 and 20 are non-representable, and the defect propagates upward indefinitely (74, 75, 218, 219, …). This happens at every doubled level, so infinitely many triples break the multiset — but scattered triples like {1,5,21} heal, which is exactly why it is not a witness. To our knowledge no object of this intermediate type appears in the literature; it may be a useful test bed, and it suggests the difficulty of (2,3) concentrates in the gap between "infinitely many breaking triples" and "all triples breaking."
Two further observations from large-scale structured search (~10⁵–10⁶ multisets across several recurrence architectures). First, a locality phenomenon: in every instance we can certify, a triple whose deletion permanently destroys completeness while all its sub-pairs heal is anchored — a consecutive window, or the floor of an exact structural resonance — and its shifted analogues higher in the sequence always heal. Second, a practical certificate that others may find useful: a deletion heals if and only if the exact subset sums of a suitable finite prefix contain an interval of width ≥ (next element − 1) at an untouched tail level; this upgrades "no gaps up to horizon 2^N" (which we found badly unreliable — we encountered false eternals surviving past 2⁵⁰) into a rigorous eventual-healing proof, and it eliminated large families of false candidates for us. In the family Aₙ₊₁ = 2Aₙ + 1 (tail values 3·2^k − 1 with multiplicity 2 and a small coin prefix), the persistent triples obey exact first-gap laws g(2^q) = α·2^q − q + C with only three values of α, verified exactly at horizons up to 2⁴⁰⁰ by a digit-DP — suggesting finite-state obstruction cycles that should be provable by automaton methods. Overall our evidence is consistent with no witness existing for any m ≥ 2 in the weak setting (mirroring van Doorn's resolution of the strict variant), with the obstruction concentrated precisely where a sequence must maintain supply exactly two above forced demand at every scale.

 If I understand correctly, the way this is formalised in Lean requires the multiset $A$ to have the property that the set
$$P(A) = \left \{\sum_{n \in B} B \subseteq A \text{ finite} \right\}$$ contains all positive integers, and a lot of texts define completeness this way. In the book by Graham and Erdős however, it is only required that $P(A)$ contains all sufficiently large integers, which is also often taken as a definition of completeness. For what it is worth, with the former interpretation that is used in the Lean formalisation I can fully settle this problem, and show that no such multiset exists for any $m, n$ with $2 \le m < n$. 
Assume $A = \{a_1, a_2 \ldots, \}$ is such that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j \}) = \mathbb{N}$ holds for all indices $i, j$. Set $s_1 = a_1$ and, for any $j \ge 2$, $s_j = a_i$ where $i$ is such that $a_{i-1} > s_1 + \ldots + s_{j-1}$. With the infinite set $S$ equal to $\{s_1, s_2, \ldots \}$, one can then check that $P(A \setminus S) = \mathbb{N}$ holds as well.
For a complete write-up, see here. Perhaps the argument can be adapted to settle the second (intended) interpretation as well.
EDIT: Come to think of it, I don't think this argument can be easily adapted to the intended interpreation, because the sequence $a_n = F_n + (-1)^n$ with $F_n$ the $n$-th Fibonacci number has the property that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j\})$ contains all large enough integers for all $i, j$, but no infinite subset $S$ exists for which $P(A \setminus S)$ contains all large enough integers. See #346 and references for more information.
EDIT 25-09-2025: I have left a comment on the Lean forum and the formalisation has now been updated to reflect the intended meaning.

A full proof 
claimed by Jesse Geneson (using GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5).
 Summary:
 I prove that only $m=0,1$ work. If every two-term deletion preserves completeness, then some deletion of any finite size does too.
 Notes:
 Here completeness means that every sufficiently large integer is a sum of finitely many terms, with each occurrence used at most once. The proof was found by Codex with GPT-6 Astra Ultra. I directed the writing and auditing workflow, then read and edited the proof and used GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5 for additional audits.
